abstract.t: A profile of RFC 4231 for nish/crypto/hmac (std/crypto/hmac.ts): HMAC () instantiated with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. Every requirement quotes RFC 4231, the main source, and every RFC 4231 test vector for those three hash functions is held here.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

nish/crypto/hmac exports one-shot HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512 over a key and a message, each as u8[]. The construction is 's; the properties compare it with nish/crypto/sha256 and nish/crypto/sha512, the hash functions it is built on. RFC 4231 also defines HMAC-SHA-224, which nish/crypto/hmac does not export.

RFC 4231 has no binding sentence in the sense of BCP 14, so there is nothing to exclude. The wiping of secret intermediates lies outside what a functional test can observe and is held by nish's own tests instead. The key blocks, hashed key, inner digest and hashers are wiped before return, held under -O2 by tests/wipes/crypto.js ("crypto_hmac crypto_hkdf: the wipes survive -O2"); the caller's own key array is recorded in docs/security/crypto-k1.md (K1-7) and docs/security/secret.md.
The module's other exports are out of scope here, each for the reason given.

Out of scope: hmacSha256Verify, an API RFC 4231 does not specify, since it defines the tag and not how one is checked; held by tests/link/crypto_hmac and tests/link/crypto_hmac_k1_verify, and the compare is timingSafeEqual, whose loop tests/cases/ct_asm_k1_ct.ts holds to no branch on the data after clang -O2 (docs/security/ct-verification.md, and docs/security/crypto-k1.md K1-8)

Out of scope: hmacSha384Verify, an API RFC 4231 does not specify, since it defines the tag and not how one is checked; held by tests/link/crypto_hmac and tests/link/crypto_hmac_k1_verify, and the compare is timingSafeEqual, whose loop tests/cases/ct_asm_k1_ct.ts holds to no branch on the data after clang -O2 (docs/security/ct-verification.md, and docs/security/crypto-k1.md K1-8)

Out of scope: hmacSha512Verify, an API RFC 4231 does not specify, since it defines the tag and not how one is checked; held by tests/link/crypto_hmac and tests/link/crypto_hmac_k1_verify, and the compare is timingSafeEqual, whose loop tests/cases/ct_asm_k1_ct.ts holds to no branch on the data after clang -O2 (docs/security/ct-verification.md, and docs/security/crypto-k1.md K1-8)

Out of scope: hmacKeyedVerify, the same check as hmacSha256Verify over an absorbed HmacKey and a window of a buffer, held by tests/link/crypto_jwt ("HmacKey: hmacKeyedVerify accepts the tag it made"); its message is a (data, off, len) /* window */, but its first parameter is the class HmacKey, which vector 0.6.0 refuses in a ts-interface block ("HmacKey is not a ts-interface type; use u8[], string, boolean, i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f64, Secret<u8[]>, u16[], u32[], u64[], each optionally | null"), and its tag is a (tag, tagAt) pair read in place, which neither a window nor an /* out CAP */ write declares
Out of scope: pbkdf2HmacSha256, PBKDF2 (RFC 8018), which uses HMAC-SHA-256 as its PRF but is a different function, with its own vectors and none in RFC 4231
Out of scope: HmacSha256, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)
Out of scope: HmacSha384, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)
Out of scope: HmacSha512, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)
Out of scope: HmacSha256Scratch, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)
Out of scope: HmacSha384Scratch, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)
Out of scope: HmacKey, a stateful, reusable form of the same functions; a property here calls only functions, so it is left to nish's own tests (tests/link/crypto_hmac*)

Out of scope: hmacKeyedInto, writes the tag of an absorbed HmacKey into a caller's array at an offset, a buffer interface RFC 4231 does not describe, held by tests/link/crypto_jwt; its message is a /* window */ and its (out, at) an /* out CAP */ write, but its first parameter is the class HmacKey, which vector 0.6.0 refuses in a ts-interface block (as for hmacKeyedVerify), and it returns void where an /* out CAP */ write returns the end offset
Out of scope: hmacCopySha256, copies a hasher's state into another, a helper for the stateful classes that computes no HMAC
Out of scope: hmacCopySha384, copies a hasher's state into another, a helper for the stateful classes that computes no HMAC
Out of scope: HMAC_SHA256, a constant that names a hash for HmacKey, not a function
Out of scope: HMAC_SHA384, a constant that names a hash for HmacKey, not a function
Out of scope: HMAC_SHA512, a constant that names a hash for HmacKey, not a function

section.name: Interface
section.sourcecode: // module: nish/crypto/hmac export const hmacSha256 = (key: u8[], data: u8[]): u8[] export const hmacSha384 = (key: u8[], data: u8[]): u8[] export const hmacSha512 = (key: u8[], data: u8[]): u8[] export const hmacSha256Secret = (key: Secret<u8[]>, data: u8[]): u8[] export const hmacSha384Secret = (key: Secret<u8[]>, data: u8[]): u8[] export const hmacSha512Secret = (key: Secret<u8[]>, data: u8[]): u8[] // module: nish/crypto/sha256 export const sha256 = (data: u8[]): u8[] // module: nish/crypto/sha512 export const sha384 = (data: u8[]): u8[] export const sha512 = (data: u8[]): u8[]

section.name: The Functions

blockquote.t: HMAC-SHA-256 is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code using the SHA-256 hash function

section.t: Note: the properties below hold hmacSha256 to the HMAC construction of over nish/crypto/sha256 (block length 64 bytes, ipad 0x36, opad 0x5c, a key longer than the block hashed first) and to a 32-byte tag.
section.sourcecode: // P-CONSTRUCTION-256 covers R-HMAC-SHA256 — HMAC-SHA-256 of a key of at most 64 bytes is the RFC 2104 construction over SHA-256 forall (key: u8[] /* 0..64 */, text: u8[] /* 0..200 */) => hmacSha256(key, text) === sha256(xor(key.concat(zeros(64 - key.length)), fill(92, 64)).concat(sha256(xor(key.concat(zeros(64 - key.length)), fill(54, 64)).concat(text))))

// P-LONG-KEY-256 covers R-HMAC-SHA256 — a key longer than 64 bytes gives the tag of its SHA-256 hash forall (key: u8[] /* 65..300 */, text: u8[] /* 0..100 */) => hmacSha256(key, text) === hmacSha256(sha256(key), text)

// P-SECRET-256 covers R-HMAC-SHA256 — hmacSha256Secret, given the key as a Secret, gives the tag hmacSha256 gives forall (key: u8[] /* 0..300 */, text: u8[] /* 0..200 */) => hmacSha256Secret(key, text) === hmacSha256(key, text)

blockquote.t: HMAC-SHA-384 is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code using the SHA-384 hash function

section.t: Note: as for SHA-256, with SHA-384, a block length of 128 bytes and a 48-byte tag.
section.sourcecode: // P-CONSTRUCTION-384 covers R-HMAC-SHA384 — HMAC-SHA-384 of a key of at most 128 bytes is the RFC 2104 construction over SHA-384 forall (key: u8[] /* 0..128 */, text: u8[] /* 0..300 */) => hmacSha384(key, text) === sha384(xor(key.concat(zeros(128 - key.length)), fill(92, 128)).concat(sha384(xor(key.concat(zeros(128 - key.length)), fill(54, 128)).concat(text))))

// P-LONG-KEY-384 covers R-HMAC-SHA384 — a key longer than 128 bytes gives the tag of its SHA-384 hash forall (key: u8[] /* 129..400 */, text: u8[] /* 0..100 */) => hmacSha384(key, text) === hmacSha384(sha384(key), text)

// P-SECRET-384 covers R-HMAC-SHA384 — hmacSha384Secret, given the key as a Secret, gives the tag hmacSha384 gives forall (key: u8[] /* 0..400 */, text: u8[] /* 0..200 */) => hmacSha384Secret(key, text) === hmacSha384(key, text)

blockquote.t: HMAC-SHA-512 is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code using the SHA-512 hash function

section.t: Note: as for SHA-256, with SHA-512, a block length of 128 bytes and a 64-byte tag.
section.sourcecode: // P-CONSTRUCTION-512 covers R-HMAC-SHA512 — HMAC-SHA-512 of a key of at most 128 bytes is the RFC 2104 construction over SHA-512 forall (key: u8[] /* 0..128 */, text: u8[] /* 0..300 */) => hmacSha512(key, text) === sha512(xor(key.concat(zeros(128 - key.length)), fill(92, 128)).concat(sha512(xor(key.concat(zeros(128 - key.length)), fill(54, 128)).concat(text))))

// P-LONG-KEY-512 covers R-HMAC-SHA512 — a key longer than 128 bytes gives the tag of its SHA-512 hash forall (key: u8[] /* 129..400 */, text: u8[] /* 0..100 */) => hmacSha512(key, text) === hmacSha512(sha512(key), text)

// P-SECRET-512 covers R-HMAC-SHA512 — hmacSha512Secret, given the key as a Secret, gives the tag hmacSha512 gives forall (key: u8[] /* 0..400 */, text: u8[] /* 0..200 */) => hmacSha512Secret(key, text) === hmacSha512(key, text)

// P-TAG-LEN covers R-HMAC-SHA256, R-HMAC-SHA384, R-HMAC-SHA512 — the tags are 32, 48 and 64 bytes, the hash output, for any key and message forall (key: u8[] /* 0..200 */, text: u8[] /* 0..200 */) => hmacSha256(key, text).length === 32 && hmacSha384(key, text).length === 48 && hmacSha512(key, text).length === 64

Test with a combined length of key and data that is larger than 64 bytes (= block-size of SHA-224 and SHA-256).

section.t: Note: Sections 4.4 and 4.5 describe test cases 3 and 4 in the same sentence; each is quoted under its own section.

front.title: Identifiers and Test Vectors for HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512

abstract.t: This document provides test vectors for the HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512 message authentication schemes. It also provides ASN.1 object identifiers and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) to identify use of these schemes in protocols. The test vectors provided in this document may be used for conformance testing. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
